clue.text: European city? Very European city

parts.note: Nice is a city on the French Riviera

explanation.surface: A puzzled repetition: someone asks about a European city and is told it is very much one.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the first 'European city' as the definition by example; the second half builds V, E and NICE, itself a European city.
explanation.definitionFit: Venice, the Italian lagoon port, is one example of a city on the Continent.

clue.text: It hurts to block extremely short pass

indicators.note: to block means the exclamation is put inside, filling the gap like a plug
short means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: extremely means very
ouch is what you say when something hurts

explanation.surface: A footballer complains of pain while blocking a pass that is far too short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' gives VERY, cut short by 'short'; 'to block' puts the cry of pain inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A voucher can be a pass or ticket granting entry or a free service.

clue.text: Set off, not worried about being famous

indicators.note: about means the remaining letters are turned round
not means the worrying word is left out

parts.note: to detonate a bomb is to set it off
ate can mean worried or troubled, as in 'what's eating you'

explanation.surface: Someone sets off, carefree about becoming a celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' is ATE as in 'what's eating you'; 'not' removes it, leaving DETON, which 'about' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means well known or celebrated, which is a synonym for famous.

clue.text: Elderly women in vehicle creating decades of tension

indicators.note: in means these pieces go inside the vehicle

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
elderly means old

explanation.surface: Old ladies in a car cause years of stress for other drivers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cold War was the decades-long standoff between the US and Soviet blocs after 1945.

clue.text: Cheered as rude tales partly rejected

indicators.note: rejected says the hidden letters are read backwards
partly says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An audience was cheered even though some of the bawdy stories were turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' hides DETALE in 'rude tales'; 'rejected' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: To be cheered is to be made happy, in high spirits, which is what elated describes.

clue.text: Place and time for insect

parts.note: a locus is a place or position

explanation.surface: Finding the right place and moment to spot a particular bug.
explanation.definitionFit: A locust is a kind of grasshopper that swarms, a well-known insect.

clue.text: More than half of lyrics inspiring surprising hit by tenor

indicators.note: by means the tenor letter is placed beside the rest
inspiring literally means breathing in, so the lyrics take the jumbled letters inside

parts.note: the lyrics of a song are its words

indicators.note: surprising suggests the letters are thrown into an unexpected order

explanation.surface: Most of a song's lyrics led to a surprise chart hit for a tenor singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprising' rearranges 'hit' to THI; 'inspiring' (breathing in) puts it inside the lyrics; 'by' sets the tenor letter alongside.
explanation.definitionFit: Two-thirds is a fraction greater than one half, so it is more than half.

clue.text: Perhaps Doris is nursing in former African kingdom

indicators.note: nursing means holding close, so the surname wraps around the other piece

parts.note: Doris Day was an American singer and actor, one example of someone named Day
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: A woman named Doris may work as a nurse somewhere in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nursing' sounds like care work but means holding: DAY holds HOME.
explanation.definitionFit: Dahomey was a West African kingdom, now the territory of Benin.

clue.text: In general, Tito abused explosive material

indicators.note: abused means misused and mistreated, so these letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Tito, the Yugoslav leader, misused explosives across the board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abused' rearranges all of IN GENERAL TITO.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitrogelatine is a gelatinous blasting explosive made from nitroglycerine, also called blasting gelatine.

clue.text: Mould stum?

definitions.meaning: an old word for mould or mustiness

explanation.surface: A cryptic question: is mould the same thing as stum?
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are obscure senses of the same short word; the question mark admits stum is a rare word.
explanation.definitionFit: Must means both mustiness or mould and new wine before fermentation, which winemakers also call stum.

clue.text: Look in idiot husband's items of underwear

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold
a clot is British slang for a fool
H is the abbreviation for husband, with the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: Someone is told to peek inside a foolish husband's drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: CLOT is everyday British slang for a stupid person.
explanation.definitionFit: Loincloths are simple wrapped garments worn over the groin, so they count as underclothes.

clue.text: Dog and pig's clothing ripped off

indicators.note: clothing means the pig word is wrapped around the other piece like a garment

parts.note: a sow is a female pig
to be had is to be cheated or ripped off

explanation.surface: A dog and a pig have had their clothes torn off them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ripped off' looks like clothes being torn away, but means cheated; 'clothing' wraps the female pig around it.
explanation.definitionFit: To dog someone is to follow them closely, exactly what a shadow or tail does.

clue.text: Faltering mother's residence ultimately here?

indicators.note: faltering means stumbling and unsteady, so these letters are knocked into a new order
ultimately points to the final letter of the next word

explanation.surface: An ailing mother might end up living in a place like this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faltering' rearranges MOTHERS into RESTHOM; 'ultimately' adds the last letter of 'residence'. The whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rest home is a care home for elderly or frail people, a likely final residence for a declining parent.

clue.text: Business's period of relative impoverishment

parts.note: broker is a jokey comparative of broke, more short of money
an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: A company is going through a spell of being less well off than before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Business's' reads as a possessive but is 'Business is'; BROKER here is the comparative of broke, not a dealer.
explanation.definitionFit: Brokerage is the trade or firm of a broker, so it can stand for a business.

clue.text: Tired before plugging art director

indicators.note: plugging means filling a gap, so this word goes inside the others

parts.note: a knack or art is a skill
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A weary film director, before the next shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: KNACKERED is British slang for exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: Knackered is informal British for utterly worn out, so it means very tired.

clue.text: Introduction of full beam leads to quarrel

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so the first letter of the word is taken

parts.note: a ray is a beam of light

explanation.surface: A driver switching on full-beam headlights starts a row with others on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A fray is a noisy fight or brawl, a sense close to quarrel.

clue.text: Bishop, when touring Italy, shows this tendency

indicators.note: touring means going round, so the first pieces wrap around the country's letter

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A bishop on a tour of Italy reveals a leaning of some kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A bias is an inclination or leaning in one direction, a synonym for tendency.

clue.text: Post made of timber found around Loch Lomond, primarily

indicators.note: found around means the timber word goes round the other letters

parts.note: a board is a piece of timber
L is the map abbreviation for loch

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so only the opening letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A wooden post stands on the shores of Loch Lomond in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found around' puts BOARD round L (Loch) and L, the first letter of 'Lomond', picked by 'primarily'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bollard is a short thick post, such as one on a quay or blocking traffic.

clue.text: Leaves female after alfresco frolicking

indicators.note: after places the female letter behind the rearranged word
frolicking means romping about playfully, so these letters are tossed into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman goes home after romping in the open air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frolicking' turns ALFRESCO into CLEARSO, and 'after' places F behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: Clears off is a casual phrasal verb meaning goes away, so it matches leaves.

clue.text: Pilot beginning to ascend using hill

indicators.note: beginning to means the first letter of the next word

parts.note: via means by way of, using
a tor is a rocky hill, especially on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A pilot starts to climb by using a hill for lift.
explanation.walkthrough: TOR is a rocky hilltop in southwest England.
explanation.definitionFit: An aviator is someone who flies aircraft, a pilot.

clue.text: One who danced well, with yen to travel

parts.note: a font is a spring or source of water, like a well

indicators.note: to travel means to move around, so these letters are shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: A fine dancer with a longing to tour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well' looks like an adverb on 'danced', but it is a noun for a water source, FONT; 'to travel' rearranges YEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Margot Fonteyn was a celebrated British ballerina, someone who danced.

clue.text: Poles stopping work making organ

indicators.note: stopping means plugging, so the poles go inside the work word

parts.note: toil is hard work
N and S are the north and south poles

explanation.surface: Polish workers walk off the job, which shapes an organ's production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like people from Poland, but means N and S.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonsil is a small mass of tissue in the throat, one of the body's organs.

clue.text: Dismissed after bar collapse

indicators.note: after places the dismissed word behind the bar word

parts.note: a Flake is a crumbly chocolate bar sold in Britain
a batsman dismissed in cricket is out

explanation.surface: Someone thrown out of a pub promptly keels over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' suggests a pub, but it is a chocolate bar: Flake is a well-known Cadbury bar in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: To flake out is informal for falling asleep or fainting from exhaustion, to collapse.

clue.text: Fish not doing very much

wordplay.note: an id, or ide, is a freshwater fish; so is a ling, so the plural fish gives both

explanation.surface: Some fish are just lazing about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' stands for two fish at once: ID (also spelt IDE) and LING.
explanation.definitionFit: Idling means passing time without work or effort.

clue.text: A lot of young men filled with love

indicators.note: filled with means the lads word holds the other letter inside

parts.note: lads are young men
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: Many youths are full of romance.
explanation.definitionFit: Loads is informal for a large amount or number, a great deal.

clue.text: Very special carcass not decomposing

indicators.note: decomposing means breaking down and rotting, so these letters fall apart into a new order

explanation.surface: A dead body that has not rotted would be remarkable indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'decomposing' rearranges the letters of CARCASS and NOT together.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacrosanct describes something regarded as too important or sacred to be interfered with.

clue.text: Excuse me! I see Australian runner removing uniform

parts.note: ah is an exclamation of understanding, like 'I see'

indicators.note: removing means the letter for uniform is taken out of the bird

parts.note: the emu is a large flightless Australian bird that runs fast
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An apology to an Australian athlete taking off their kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Australian runner' is not an athlete but the emu; 'removing' drops its U.
explanation.definitionFit: Ahem is the small cough used to attract attention politely, much like saying excuse me.

clue.text: It's easy to swindle Oscar for one

indicators.note: for means one letter stands in the place of the other

parts.note: to diddle is British slang for to swindle or cheat
I is the Roman numeral for one
O is Oscar in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Cheating an Oscar winner turns out to be simple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar for one' looks like an example of an award; read it as O replacing I (one) in DIDDLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A doddle is British slang for a very easy task, something that is a breeze.

clue.text: Nick's spin is working

parts.note: PR, public relations, is the business of spin
on means operating or working

explanation.surface: A man called Nick puts a political spin on things that works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a name, but it is British slang for prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick is British slang for jail, as in 'banged up in the nick'.
